node-1.label: Patient presented with bouts of extremely stiff, nonpainful neck with involuntary head tilting leftwards, upwards, and backwards in hyperextension

node-2.label: 19-year-old female student (weight 35 kg, height 159 cm) was admitted with grade III dyspnea

node-3.label: Post-surgery she was prescribed diuretics (spironolactone–torsemide combination) and aspirin; a new medication was started at low dose 25 mg/day divided into two doses for two days, then increased to 25 mg twice daily on the third day

node-4.label: She was discharged on the fifth postoperative day but readmitted the same evening

node-5.label: Physical examination also showed conjugate deviation of the eyes upward or laterally, involuntary posturing with head, neck, and spine arched backward, and difficulty opening or closing the mouth

why.why: Laboratory expert analysis reinforces the temporal link to recent drug escalation, low body weight, same-day readmission, and classic signs (stiff neck, upward eye deviation, opisthotonos, difficulty opening mouth), concluding that drug-induced acute dystonia is the leading diagnosis. Although definitive confirmation remains pending (medication reconciliation, anticholinergic response, CSF exclusion), no competing evidence has emerged; therefore confidence is modestly increased from 0.85 to 0.88.

attrs.why: node-5 shows overlapping signs such as opisthotonos and mouth difficulty; node-3 new medication and nonpainful course refute a primary infectious cause.
No direct evidence supports this; organic drug-related signs and temporal drug link make psychogenic cause unlikely.

node-9.label: Laboratory expert analysis states that the temporal link, low weight, same-day readmission, and classic signs strongly support drug-induced acute dystonia, with definitive confirmation still pending
